title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia as CEO after scandal
description:
Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO was followed by to a surge in the tech company's stock — and the stock market.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: Nvidia's stock rose more than 30% yesterday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: In fact, the entire stock market rallied. The indexes had already been pointing upward before the news and then soared. Nvidia's stock alone increased in value by just under $1 trillion.MARTIN: Our colleague, Ricky Mulvey, with The Indicator From Planet Money, our daily economic podcast, is with us now to tell us more. Good morning, Ricky.RICKY MULVEY, BYLINE: Good morning.MARTIN: So why are investors so happy about Jensen Huang coming back?MULVEY: Well, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. Investors were happy to put the scandals aside and said that Jensen Huang is a good chunk of the company's value. And that boost, about $950 billion of market cap, is the biggest one-day gain for a single company ever. And for context, that's in the ballpark of all of Walmart's stock, who, as you may know, is the largest private sector employer in the United States.MARTIN: So as you've said, and you're not the only person to say this, that Jensen Huang is Nvidia, how does that translate into the broader market?MULVEY: Well, Jensen is one of the chief storytellers and central bankers in the AI economy. So much of the stock market now is a bet on artificial intelligence, and Jensen Huang has persuasively told investors why this bet is a good one, saying AI will create high-paying jobs and fundamentally change the economy.MARTIN: And Nvidia is an important player in that AI economy for companies other than itself.MULVEY: Exactly. Nvidia has its hands in a lot of these circular financing deals, but we'll look at neoclouds for a second. And these are smaller data center companies betting big on AI. One of these is a company called CoreWeave. Now, this company takes out a lot of debt, buys Nvidia chips and then rents out computing space to customers. And debt investors believe that CoreWeave is super risky. In fact, back in October, MarketWatch said that credit investors implied that CoreWeave had a better-than-average chance of going bankrupt over the next five years. CoreWeave lost hundreds of millions of dollars last quarter after it made interest payments.However, Nvidia has a deal with CoreWeave. If CoreWeave can't find customers, Nvidia will pay for computing power themselves. In other words, it's like an auto manufacturer leasing cars from the dealerships to make sure those dealerships can stay in business. Also CoreWeave's stock rose 22% yesterday with Jensen Huang's return.MARTIN: Do investors believe that Nvidia has a lot of growth ahead?MULVEY: You know, surprisingly, not really. Nvidia stock trades at about 10 times forward earnings, and that means stock investors say they only want to pay for 10 years' worth of future profits right now. And investors are willing to pay more for other chipmakers, implying they have more growth coming in the future. In the stock market, Nvidia's multiple is pretty low. It's in the same neighborhood as a company like Kroger, which is a more stodgy, predictable grocery store chain, not exactly a high-flying chipmaker. So even with this huge boost, Nvidia's investors aren't predicting much growth ahead, even though the company just doubled its sales over the last year.MARTIN: But outside of what investors predict, this company is huge - I mean, the second-largest on the stock market. Now, too big to fail is something that we heard in the recession. It's bubbling up now with Nvidia. Is it applicable here?MULVEY: It seems that way. The vast majority of AI workloads run on Nvidia chips. Its technology is putting together images of black holes, making self-driving cars run, even putting brains into humanoid robots. This is the technology that's supposed to make the circular financing and mountains of debt all worth it. And Nvidia very much runs that technology. And the stock market seemed to say it wants Jensen Huang running Nvidia, no matter the personal indiscretions, questionable management style or the national security implications.MARTIN: That is Ricky Mulvey. He's part of the team that makes The Indicator From Planet Money, NPR's daily economic podcast. Ricky, thank you.MULVEY: Thank you. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
